patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral foot and hand numbness, tingling, and weakness progressing over 2 years
patient.history_present_illness: A 58-year-old retired administrative assistant with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.2%) and recently diagnosed undertreated hypothyroidism was referred to neurology for progressive bilateral numbness and tingling. She describes onset of bilateral foot tingling approximately two years ago, initially subtle and attributed to 'sitting cross-legged.' Over the following year the tingling progressed up both legs to the knee, and burning pain began affecting both feet at night, interfering with sleep. Approximately eight months ago she noticed tingling spreading to her fingertips bilaterally, predominantly in the fourth and fifth fingers of both hands. She has noticed her handwriting has become slightly shaky. She dropped a cup of coffee six months ago due to grip weakness. She has had difficulty with buttons and zippers. She saw her internist four months ago, who found her TSH to be 12.4 mIU/L (newly elevated, undertreated) and started her on levothyroxine at a low dose; her most recent TSH three weeks ago was 6.8 mIU/L — still significantly elevated. She has had persistently elevated HbA1c despite oral agent therapy. She was referred for neurology evaluation of bilateral peripheral neuropathy.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, fully oriented. Mild cognitive slowing — she reports difficulty concentrating.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild intrinsic hand weakness bilaterally (4/5 grip, 4+/5 APB). Mild bilateral toe extensor weakness (4/5 EHL). No wrist drop or foot drop.
neurological_exam.sensory: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss — bilateral feet to knees (severe), bilateral hands to mid-forearm (moderate). Vibration severely reduced at both great toes and ankles, mildly reduced at fingertips bilaterally. Proprioception reduced at bilateral great toes.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Knee jerks 1+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis and biceps 2+. Plantar flexors bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild sensory ataxia on heel-shin. Finger-nose slightly clumsy bilaterally (sensory).
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly wide-based. Steppage component bilateral. Romberg positive.
neurological_exam.additional: No pes cavus. Mild bilateral pitting edema ankles (hypothyroidism). Dry skin, mildly coarse hair.

Neuropathy_workup.value: No M-spike; polyclonal IgG mild elevation

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL (L), Glucose 186 mg/dL (H), HbA1c 9.2 % (H), TSH 6.8 mIU/L (H), Free T4 0.7 ng/dL (L), Vitamin B12 182 pg/mL (L), MMA 0.42 umol/L (H), ANA 1:80 (speckled)  (H).
abnormal_values_summary: ANA 1: 80 (weakly positive — thyroid-associated, no specific antibodies) (H)

specialized_test.test_type: Nerve conduction studies and EMG — bilateral upper and lower extremities

findings.pattern: Severely reduced amplitude, mildly slow velocity — axonal with secondary demyelination (hypothyroid component)
Mildly reduced amplitude — early upper extremity involvement (glove component)
Mildly reduced amplitude — consistent with glove distribution

quantitative_data.pattern: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy — bilateral, glove-and-stocking distribution

specialized_test.impression: Moderate length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy in a glove-and-stocking distribution. SNAP amplitudes reduced bilaterally in sural and superficial peroneal nerves, with mild slowing of conduction velocities. Upper extremity sensory NCS mildly reduced in median and ulnar distributions. Motor CMAP amplitudes reduced in bilateral lower extremity nerves. EMG shows chronic active denervation in distal lower and upper extremity musculature. Findings are consistent with a moderate length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Hypothyroid neuropathy — reversibility with thyroid hormone replacement
results.key_finding: Hypothyroid neuropathy partially reverses with adequate thyroid replacement (TSH target 1-3 mIU/L); improvement may take 3-6 months; incomplete reversal if longstanding

output.summary: Hypothyroid polyneuropathy is a recognized, potentially reversible neuropathy associated with untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism. Thyroid hormone replacement leads to partial or full reversal in a subset of patients; improvement may take months. The degree of reversibility is related to the severity and duration of hypothyroidism prior to treatment.

output.proposed: Cyanocobalamin supplementation for B12 deficiency on metformin
interactions: Metformin reduces B12 absorption via ileal mechanism
warnings: Annual B12 monitoring required while on metformin
Oral cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily is effective for metformin-associated B12 deficiency

findings.finding: Reduced bilateral — autonomic small fiber involvement
Mildly reduced HRV — borderline cardiac autonomic neuropathy

output.impression: Mild sudomotor dysfunction bilaterally on QSART. Mildly reduced heart rate variability on deep breathing. Findings indicate mild autonomic dysfunction in a distal-predominant pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: Duloxetine for neuropathic pain in T2DM + hypothyroidism
interactions: No significant interactions with levothyroxine, metformin, or amlodipine
warnings: Duloxetine is first-line FDA-approved for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain
Monitor BP with duloxetine — patient on amlodipine for hypertension

findings.finding: Bilateral sensory loss — monofilament absent at plantar surfaces. No current ulcers. Mild dry skin.

output.impression: Absent protective sensation bilaterally on 10g monofilament testing. No current ulcerations. Mild dry skin bilaterally. Findings indicate high-risk foot status with loss of protective sensation. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Mixed-etiology peripheral polyneuropathy (diabetic + hypothyroid + B12 deficiency)

differential.key_features: TSH 6.8 (mildly elevated); treat with levothyroxine titration.
Axonal pattern would argue against; need demyelinating features.
No family history or pes cavus.

optimal_actions.action: Order broad neuropathy labs (CBC, CMP, HbA1c, B12 + MMA, TSH, SPEP/IFE, urinalysis)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify reversible/treatable etiologies (diabetes, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, thyroid disease)

optimal_actions.action: Order EMG/NCS to characterize axonal vs demyelinating pattern and distribution
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Length-dependent axonal vs demyelinating vs multifocal pattern; severity and distribution

optimal_actions.action: Search literature for DSP evaluation guidelines and etiology-specific recommendations
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirm AAN 2009 DSP workup, etiology-specific evaluations

optimal_actions.action: Review medications for neurotoxic agents and check interactions for symptomatic therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify potentially neurotoxic drugs (chemotherapy, metronidazole, megadose B6, nitrofurantoin); guide neuropathic-pain pharmacotherapy

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Treat all three contributing etiologies (diabetic, hypothyroid, B12 deficiency)
Symptomatic neuropathic pain therapy if needed
contraindicated_actions: Do not address only one contributor and ignore the others
key_reasoning_points: Multifactorial neuropathy is common; identify ALL contributors and treat each
Hypothyroidism and B12 deficiency are reversible contributors; do not miss them
